why: Moment bounds Σ f(n)^k with sharp exponents constrain the distribution of R(p).
first_step: Compute numerically Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n)^2, f(n)^3 and fit exponents of log N; compare with decoupling-type predictions.
refs: Wooley, Nested efficient congruencing and relatives of Vinogradov's mean value theorem, Proc. LMS 118 (2019)

title: Holowinsky–Soundararajan: sieve + subconvexity combo for 'large on average, so not zero' at one form
connection: Holowinsky–Soundararajan proved mass equidistribution for holomorphic Hecke forms by combining two weak methods (sieve bounds for shifted sums, Soundararajan's weak subconvexity) that each fail alone; ES's pointwise lower tail resists every single method.
why: Template for 'two complementary partial methods cover all cases' — e.g. one method for p with many small factors in 4Cp+1, another for the rest.
first_step: Split hard primes by an 'anatomy' parameter (e.g. number of small prime factors of the first slices) and check whether different repo methods cover complementary regimes.
refs: Holowinsky–Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms, Ann. Math. 172 (2010)

title: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh small solutions to linear congruences
connection: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh study the distribution of the smallest solution of linear congruences via equidistribution of lattices; ES certificates are small solutions of congruences with modulus tied to p.
why: Gives the limiting distribution of 'smallest certificate size', comparable with ES's forced windows.
first_step: Write the ES Type II certificate as a small solution of a linear congruence system mod 4cd and compare its size distribution with SV's limit law.
refs: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh, Small solutions to linear congruences and Hecke equidistribution, Acta Arith. 118 (2005)

title: Katz equidistribution of Kloosterman angles for fixed-modulus ES counts
connection: Katz: Kloosterman angles at a fixed prime modulus equidistribute w.r.t. Sato–Tate as the argument varies; ES fixed-modulus counts (FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS) reduce to Kloosterman-type sums.
why: Gives exact variance/distribution of ES residue counts across p mod ℓ.
first_step: Compute the ES count mod a prime ℓ as a function of p mod ℓ and test Sato–Tate statistics of its fluctuating part.
refs: Katz, Gauss Sums, Kloosterman Sums, and Monodromy Groups (1988)

title: Rudnick–Soundararajan lower bounds for moments → 'at least one large term'
connection: Rudnick–Soundararajan prove lower bounds for moments of L-function families by a simple Hölder trick; ES needs lower bounds for a count of certificates.
why: Moment lower bounds (≥ expected order) for R(p) over a C-family at fixed p would show certificates are not all absent — but only if the family is at fixed p.
first_step: Apply the RS Hölder trick to Σ_C R_C(p) with weights and see whether it gives Σ_C R_C(p) ≫ main term at a single p.
refs: Rudnick–Soundararajan, Lower bounds for moments of L-functions, PNAS 102 (2005)

title: Interval/ball arithmetic certified analytic constants (Arb/FLINT) for explicit exceptional sets
connection: Arb provides rigorous numerics; explicit versions of the repo's exceptional-set or main-term constants need certified evaluation of Euler products and integrals.
why: Needed for any explicit statement (calibration with verification).
first_step: Compute M_BM(p)'s Euler-product constant with Arb to 30 digits with certified error.
refs: Johansson, Arb: efficient arbitrary-precision midpoint-radius interval arithmetic, IEEE Trans. Comput. 66 (2017)

title: OAI 007 ordinary two-point Chowla (claimed) for λ-weighted ES counts
connection: OAI 007 claims Σ_{n≤X} λ(a₁n+b₁)λ(a₂n+b₂) ≪ X/(log X)^c for fixed affine forms; ES certificate counts can be twisted by λ of the p-tied integers to detect parity structure.
why: Parity of Ω(4Cp+1) correlates with whether its divisors can split into classes; ordinary (non-log) two-point Chowla removes the log-averaging that blocked earlier transfers.
first_step: Check whether 'number of divisors ≡ −1 (mod 4) of N' correlates with λ(N) for N in an AP, and if so formulate the needed correlation along the forms (4Cp+1, 4C′p+1).

title: Iwaniec / Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao Jacobsthal & large-gap sieves for sterile windows
connection: Large-gap constructions (FGKMT) sieve out long intervals by choosing residue classes cleverly; ES sterile windows (all slices in a window fail) are analogous 'sieved-out' intervals.
why: The machinery (hypergraph covering, Maynard weights) for building long sifted intervals tells how long a sterile slice window could be.
first_step: Compute the longest run of failing e-slices at hard primes and compare with a FGKMT-type construction of residue classes killing a window.
refs: Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao, Long gaps between primes, JAMS 31 (2018)

title: OAI 024 asymptotic count of totients (claimed) — value-set counting technique
connection: OAI 024 claims an asymptotic for V(x) = #{φ(n) ≤ x}; Ford's anatomy of totients machinery counts value sets of multiplicative functions — ES's 'set of n with an ES solution of shape S' is a value set problem.
why: Value-set counting with structured preimages mirrors 'set of 4/n reachable by shape S'.
first_step: Read OAI 024 introduction for the method and see if 'n = 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' value-set counting fits.
refs: Ford, The distribution of totients, Ramanujan J. 2 (1998)

title: Sawin square-root cancellation for factorisation-type functions in short intervals over 𝔽_q[T]
connection: Sawin proved square-root cancellation for sums of arithmetic functions depending on factorisation type in very short intervals over 𝔽_q[T]; 'has a divisor in a class' depends on factorisation plus residues.
why: Short-interval control over 𝔽_q[T] is exactly the slice-window statement needed in a function-field ES lower tail.
first_step: Check whether 'N has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod M)' is a 'factorisation function' in Sawin's sense (it depends on residues of factors, so needs his twisted version).
refs: Sawin, Square-root cancellation for sums of factorization functions over short intervals in function fields, Duke Math. J. 170 (2021)

title: Turán–Kubilius inequality for R(p) across C: second-moment pointwise statements
connection: Turán–Kubilius bounds variance of additive functions; R_C(p) summed over C is a sum of divisor-class indicators, whose variance over C at fixed p might be bounded by a Turán–Kubilius-type argument.
why: A variance bound Var_C ≪ (mean)² /K at fixed p would imply many C succeed — pointwise in p, averaged over C.
first_step: Compute mean and variance over C ≤ X of R_C(p) at hard primes; test whether Var/mean² decays with X.

title: Ford–Konyagin–Luca / multiplicative structure of shifted primes p+e for e-slice generators
connection: Results on prime factors of shifted primes (Baker–Harman largest prime factor of p−1, Fouvry; Erdős–Pomerance) control whether N_e = (p+e)/4 has many small factors (good for generating −1).
why: Shifted-prime anatomy across all p is known in averaged forms; a fixed-p statement over e is needed.
first_step: Compute the fraction of hard primes p for which the first 10 slices N_e are all y-rough (no factors ≤ y) and compare with independence.
refs: Baker–Harman, Shifted primes without large prime factors, Acta Arith. 83 (1998)

title: Heath-Brown delta-method circle method for Σ_{n≤N} f(n) with power saving
connection: Heath-Brown's delta method counts integral points on quadrics/cubics with Kloosterman refinement; the total count of ES solutions over n ≤ N is an integral-point count on the 3-fold 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx).
why: Power-saving asymptotics for the total count, and for counts restricted to n in APs, feed variance and exceptional-set arguments.
first_step: Set up the delta-method count for #{(n,x,y,z): n ≤ N} with a smooth weight and identify the singular series (should match ET's main term).
refs: Heath-Brown, A new form of the circle method, and its application to quadratic forms, J. reine angew. Math. 481 (1996)

title: Munshi's delta-method variants (DFI δ with conductor lowering) for ES character sums
connection: Munshi's conductor-lowering trick proves subconvexity by inserting extra averaging; ES counts at fixed p could use an artificial extra average (over a dummy modulus) to gain cancellation.
why: Conductor lowering creates averages where none exist — precisely ES's 'no free average' problem.
first_step: Insert a dummy average over auxiliary primes q ~ Q into the fixed-p ES count expansion and see whether Poisson summation yields a gain.
refs: Munshi, The circle method and bounds for L-functions III: t-aspect subconvexity for GL(3) L-functions, JAMS 28 (2015)

title: Tao–Teräväinen odd-order log-Chowla & Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen sign patterns
connection: Tao–Teräväinen proved odd-order log-averaged Chowla; KMT studied sign patterns of multiplicative functions; ES certificates at consecutive slices involve λ/divisor patterns of consecutive integers N, N+1, …
why: Patterns of multiplicative data on consecutive integers are exactly what Type II slices are.
first_step: Tabulate (λ(N_e), λ(N_{e+4}), …) patterns at hard primes vs random and test for bias.
refs: Tao–Teräväinen, The structure of logarithmically averaged correlations of multiplicative functions, with applications to the Chowla and Elliott conjectures, Duke Math. J. 168 (2019)

title: Gallagher's larger sieve with prime-power moduli to bound sterile p
connection: The larger sieve bounds sets missing many residue classes modulo prime powers; sterile primes must lie in non-covered classes modulo many moduli 4C simultaneously.
why: A direct quantitative bound on the number of primes ≤ X sterile to depth K.
first_step: Compute, for each modulus m ≤ M, the number of residue classes of p that are sterile for certificates of modulus m, and plug into the larger sieve.
refs: Gallagher, A larger sieve, Acta Arith. 18 (1971)
Croot–Elsholtz, On variants of the larger sieve, Acta Math. Hungar. 103 (2004)

title: Selberg Λ² upper-bound sieve for the number of sterile p ≤ X at depth K
connection: Λ² sieve gives sharp upper bounds for sifted sets; 'p sterile for all certificates with C ≤ K' is a sifting condition on p modulo the moduli 4C and auxiliary primes.
why: Gives E_K(X) ≪ X/(log X)^{g(K)} with explicit g, the cleanest depth-K exceptional bound.
first_step: Compute the sieve dimension of the depth-K sterility condition from the densities of sterile classes mod primes ℓ.

title: Kloosterman/KMS bounds applied to the I3 count averaged over t
connection: I3's divisor event involves tn+1 with class −1 mod t; averaging over t ≤ T at fixed n gives Kloosterman-type sums with modulus t (small).
why: Fixed-n averages over t is the I3 analogue of fixed-p averages over C — test bed for bilinear Kloosterman input.
first_step: Write Σ_t Σ_{d | tn+1} 1_{d ≡ −1 (t)} via Fourier in d mod t and identify the Kloosterman sums.

title: Green–Sawhney-type Type II information for p² + 4c²d with d prime
connection: Restricting to prime d makes p² + 4c²d a sparse polynomial family close to Green–Sawhney's p² + nq² setting.
why: Sub-family selection to reach a known bilinear estimate; the count loses only a log factor.
first_step: Measure how often Type I certificates with d prime exist at p ≤ 10^7.

title: Rosser–Iwaniec semi-linear sieve for I3 at t = 4: 'tn+1 has a divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4)'
connection: At t = 4, the I3 event needs a divisor of 4n+1 that is ≡ −1 (mod 4) (plus size constraints): it fails iff all prime factors of 4n+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) — a semi-linear sifted set of density ≍ (log n)^{−1/2}.
why: Exact density of the t = 4 failure set; combining t = 4, 8, 12 … failures gives a sieve-dimension computation for I3's exceptional set.
first_step: Compute the joint failure probability for t ∈ {4, 8, 12, 16} under independence and compare with data.

title: Effective Chebotarev in the ES Type I ray class fields (explicit success density per (c,d))
connection: For fixed (c,d), the density of primes p having a Type I certificate with that (c,d) and a prime f is a Chebotarev density in a field tied to (c,d); summing gives M_BM's constant.
why: Explicit densities let one compute the exact main term and the variance contributed by each (c,d).
first_step: Compute the Chebotarev density for (c,d) ∈ {(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)} via PARI and compare with empirical frequencies.
refs: Lagarias–Odlyzko, Effective versions of the Chebotarev density theorem (1977)

title: Vinogradov's least-QNR conjecture as a sufficient hypothesis for the BM layer only
connection: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9: the BM layer is pointwise free, i.e. some level 4 | t ≤ 4ℓ(p) has a positive main term. The remaining question is the class of the divisor inside a coset. Least-QNR bounds control the first layer only.
why: This calibrates what 'standard conjectures' buy; the second layer needs a different hypothesis (equidistribution of divisor classes of one integer).
first_step: Formulate the minimal second-layer hypothesis ('divisors of tp+1 equidistribute in (ℤ/t)^× for some t ≤ T') and compare it with the known Erdős–Hall/Montgomery-type results on divisor class distribution.

title: Kloosterman-sum form of the word count R_t(p) and Weil-bound positivity
connection: #{(X,Y): XY = tp+1, X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (t), sizes} is a divisor-in-progression count. Its sign-twisted version Σ(A/p) is a sum of Jacobi symbols over divisors, expressible by Kloosterman/Salié sums after Poisson summation.
why: Weil's bound is the native positivity tool. It needs long sums, and the word count per level is O(1), which is the B3 issue in native terms.
first_step: Write the χ-twisted level-t count as a Salié sum expression and record the length vs modulus ratio.

title: Burgess-type bounds for character sums over 'divisor sets' (multiplicative structure)
connection: ES₅ needs χ_p to be non-constant on S₃(p) = {A : r(p/A) = 3}, a set of size ≈ log²p built from divisors. Character sums over multiplicatively structured sets (products of two sets) admit Burgess/bilinear bounds.
why: S₃(p) = {(p+u)/v : v | p+u, …}: if it contains a product set A·B mod p with |A|,|B| ≫ p^ε, bilinear character-sum bounds would force a non-residue.
first_step: Check computationally whether S₃(p) (or the larger S_L(p)) contains large product sets A·B mod p.

title: Height zeta function of the threefold 𝒰 and its analytic continuation
connection: Σ_{(n,x,y,z) ∈ 𝒰(ℤ_{>0})} H(n,x,y,z)^{−s} counts all ES solutions. Its rightmost pole gives the log²-order average count (ET). Its analytic structure, e.g. as a sum of Eisenstein-type series via the torsor, is native to Manin-conjecture methods (Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel).
why: Analytic continuation gives secondary terms, which control the lower tail in short intervals of n, a step towards almost-all-with-rates.
first_step: Write the height zeta function via ET's parametrisation as a multiple Dirichlet series and identify its polar structure.
refs: Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel, Igusa integrals and volume asymptotics (2010)

title: Bohr-set formulation: L₃(p) as elements of a multiplicative Bohr set intersected with an exact divisibility condition
connection: A ∈ L₃(p) ⇔ A ≡ u·v⁻¹ (mod p), A = (p+u)/v, so, precisely, A/p = 1/v + u/(pv), the right endpoint of (1/v, 1/v + u/(pv)], so A lies in a union of short intervals near 1/v (a Bohr-type set for the frequencies 1/v) and is exactly determined there. ES₅ asks for a QNR in this union with exact landing.
why: Character sums over Bohr sets (Burgess-type in short intervals near rationals with small denominators) are native. Exact landing is again the divisor condition, but the interval structure may give partial control.
first_step: Compute the union of intervals I_v = (p/v, p/v + u/v)-type for all (u,v) and its total length vs p; compare with Burgess thresholds.

title: Vinogradov bilinear decomposition of the (★) count
connection: Vinogradov's Type I/II bilinear sums made ternary Goldbach unconditional. R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 (4C)} is a sum over factorizations ab = 4Cp+1; split by the sizes of a, b, C into 'Type I' (one factor short: congruence sums in C) and 'Type II' (both medium: bilinear forms in (a,b)).
why: Gives a structured place where cancellation must be found; the Type I part may be treatable pointwise in p by elementary counting.
first_step: Write R(p) = Σ_{a,b} α_a β_b 1[ab ≡ 1 mod 4C, ab = 4Cp+1] with dyadic ranges; compute numerically which range carries the solutions for p ~ 10⁸–10¹⁰.

title: Almost-prime levels: choose C with 4Cp+1 = q₁q₂ (two primes) and study the class of q₁ mod 4C
connection: Chen-type results produce almost-primes in linear sequences. If 4Cp+1 = q₁q₂, the certificate condition at level C is q₁ ≡ −1 (mod 4C), a single-prime class condition.
why: Reduces a divisor-class problem to an equidistribution question for prime factors of almost-primes in a progression, a better-studied object.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁸ and C ≤ 10⁵ measure: fraction of C with 4Cp+1 = P₂, and the rate at which a factor hits −1 mod 4C versus the model 2/φ(4C).

title: Divisor function in APs to a single modulus 4p as the base asymptotic
connection: Σ_{C≤X} τ(4Cp+1) is a divisor sum in the progression 1 mod 4p; asymptotics are known for X ≥ (4p)^{2/3+ε} (Selberg/Hooley/Heath-Brown/Fouvry–Iwaniec-type). The ES count refines τ to the class d ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
why: Starts from a pointwise-in-p theorem that is already true, and asks for a twist by the 'self-referential' modulus 4C — a precise, new-looking question.
first_step: Write D(4Cp+1; −1 mod 4C) via additive characters mod 4C and apply Voronoi summation in C to the twisted divisor sum; identify which terms are new.
refs: Linnik, The dispersion method in binary additive problems (AMS 1963)

title: Kloosterman refinement in the level variable t for Σ_t D_t^−(tp+1)
connection: Kloosterman's refinement made 4-variable forms work by averaging Kloosterman sums over the Farey denominators. The all-level ES count Σ_t D_t^−(tp+1) is a divisor problem whose Fourier expansion in t produces Kloosterman sums (cf. the Type I Heegner/Kuznetsov note).
why: Kuznetsov is already used for the Type I sum; applying it to the level sum at fixed p is the pointwise version.
first_step: Write Σ_{t≤T} D_t^−(tp+1) via additive characters, identify the Kloosterman sums S(m,n;c), and estimate their contribution using Weil + Kuznetsov for fixed p.

title: Linnik with a varying auxiliary split prime: ℓ = least prime with prescribed (p/ℓ)
connection: Linnik's ergodic method needed (−n/ℓ) = 1 for a fixed ℓ; varying ℓ with n is how one covers every n if the method is uniform in ℓ. ES: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 shows the BM layer is pointwise free using the least ℓ with (n/ℓ) = −1; find an ℓ-adic dynamical argument for certificates using that ℓ.
why: Bounded ℓ ≤ 4ℓ(n) is already known to suffice for BM positivity; a dynamical/Hecke argument at that ℓ could control the next layer.
first_step: Look for an ℓ-Hecke correspondence on ES certificates (e.g. on the quaternion/SL₂ form: matrices of determinant ℓ acting on [[a,p],[c,d]]) and test whether it maps certificates of p to certificates of p.
refs: Einsiedler-Lindenstrauss-Michel-Venkatesh, Ann. Math. 173 (2011) (Distribution of periodic torus orbits and Duke's theorem for cubic fields) / Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems (Duke's theorem and Linnik's ergodic method)

title: Many-variable relaxations: ES with an extra term tied to the others
connection: Hasse principle holds for forms in many variables (Davenport, Heath-Brown, Hooley). 4-term ES is trivial; find intermediate 'k-term ES with constraints' (e.g. 1/x+1/y+1/z+1/w with w forced to equal xyz·k, or two terms merging 1/a+1/b = 1/c) that are circle-method accessible and imply 3-term ES.
why: Interpolates between trivial (4 free terms) and hard (3 terms); the implication step is the interesting part.
first_step: List 4-term constrained families and for each check (i) does a solution give a 3-term solution, (ii) number of variables after eliminating constraints.
refs: Davenport, Phil. Trans. A 251 (1959)/ Proc. Roy. Soc. A 272 (1963)

title: A certificate scheme whose only hard condition is primality of linear forms (Green–Tao–Ziegler unconditional)
connection: Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg made Hypothesis-H-conditional fibration arguments unconditional when only linear polynomials must be prime, via Green–Tao–Ziegler. ES: search for a certificate parametrisation where, for fixed p, it suffices that a finite system of linear forms in free auxiliary variables be simultaneously prime.
why: GTZ would then give infinitely many such auxiliary tuples for each p — an unconditional every-p mechanism. Thm C (bounded witnesses fail under H) does not obviously forbid unbounded prime-based witnesses.
first_step: Enumerate ES certificate shapes where a denominator or factor is a free prime (e.g. Type I f prime, window prime q) and check whether remaining conditions can be made linear in auxiliary variables.

title: Dirichlet's product trick: a product of all level series with nonnegative coefficients
connection: Dirichlet: Π_χ L(s,χ) = ζ_K(s) has nonnegative coefficients, so no L(1,χ) vanishes. ES: look for a product/combination of the twisted level series Σ_χ σ_χ(tn+1) whose coefficients are nonnegative and whose value 'at s = 1' (or at the p-th coefficient) is forced positive.
why: Positivity of a combination is how non-vanishing statements are proved for every modulus; METAPLECTIC Thm K gives exactly these character-twisted series.
first_step: From Thm K, form Σ_{χ mod t} σ_χ(N) products over a few levels t and test numerically which combinations have nonnegative coefficients that vanish at p only when R(p) = 0.

title: Harman-style comparison sieve: R(p) versus the average of R(n) over a short interval around p
connection: Harman's sieve gets primes in every short interval by comparing a decomposition with a model where asymptotics are known, discarding only small nonnegative terms. ES: compare R(p) with ⟨R(n)⟩ over n ∈ [p−H, p+H] in the same residue class mod 840, using Type I/II information on the multiplicative structure of 4Cn+1.
why: Averages of R over short intervals are accessible (E(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4})); the comparison step is the pointwise-transfer mechanism.
first_step: Numerically measure |R(p) − ⟨R⟩_H|/⟨R⟩_H for H = p^θ, θ = 0.1..0.5, and see which H makes the comparison tight.

title: Large-values / 'zero-density' estimate for levels at fixed p
connection: Hoheisel's every-interval theorem needed that few zeros are far right (zero density). ES analogue: at fixed p, show that only few levels C have a large deviation of the level count D_C(p) from its expected 2/φ(4C)·(…), so the many 'good' levels carry R(p) > 0.
why: Large-values estimates are statements about one object (here one p) and many 'frequencies' (levels) — the right quantifier order.
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of level deviations for fixed p ~ 10⁹ and test a large-values inequality of the shape #{C ≤ X : |dev_C| > V} ≪ X·(stuff)/V².

title: Burgess shift trick on the level variable
connection: Burgess amplifies a short character sum by shifting n → n + ab and using multiplicativity. ES events at level C involve the residue of 4Cp+1 modulo divisors; shifting C → C + kd preserves 'd | 4Cp+1'. Use shifts to relate the certificate count on a short C-range to a complete sum handled by Weil.
why: A Burgess-type argument for divisor events in a short level range would give certificates with small C (C ≤ p^{1/4+ε}), a pointwise statement.
first_step: Write #{C ≤ X : ∃ d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} with d in a fixed range as a character sum over C mod d and try the (n + ab) shift with Hölder.

title: Profinite zero–one law for ES certificate sets
connection: Gallagher's zero–one law makes metric Diophantine sets have measure 0 or 1. In the profinite completion of ℤ, the set of p̂ admitting a certificate at a finite level is open; its complement is closed of Haar measure 0 (almost-all theorem). Characterise the complement (contains square-mimicking points, B1).
why: The integers are a countable dense subset; ES says no integer lies in the closed null set. Knowing its exact shape (squares only? more?) is the profinite form of the problem.
first_step: Compute, for M = 840·k with k ≤ 30, the residues mod M not covered by certificates with all parameters dividing powers of M; compare with the squares mod M.

title: Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec well-factorable weights for the 'self-referential modulus'
connection: BFI pushed level of distribution beyond 1/2 for well-factorable weights. ES events have modulus 4C that is itself a factor of the divisor equation (d ≡ −1 mod 4C with d | 4Cp+1); exploit factorability of the weights in C.
why: The self-referential modulus is ES's distinctive structure; BFI-type dispersion is designed for moduli with flexible factorizations.
first_step: Rewrite R(p) with C = C₁C₂ factorable weights and check whether the resulting sums fit the BFI dispersion template (sum over moduli of a fixed residue).

title: Transference principle: dense subsets of ES certificates relative to a pseudorandom majorant
connection: Green–Tao: a dense subset of a pseudorandom set inherits linear patterns. ES certificate sets for varying p sit inside the majorant {all factorizations of 4Cp+1}; transference could show a positive-density subset of p's certificate data forces patterns that are certificates for other p's.
why: Odd: it moves information between different p, which is not ES; but a pattern-based closure (certificate for p₁,p₂ ⇒ certificate for p₃) would be an every-type mechanism.
first_step: Search the (★) data for linear patterns: triples (p₁,p₂,p₃) in AP whose certificates are linearly related.
refs: arXiv:math/0404188 (Green-Tao, primes contain arbitrarily long APs)

title: Almost-all exponents → all: Faltings-type finiteness for ES failure configurations
connection: Heath-Brown/Granville deduced FLT for almost all exponents from Faltings' finiteness. ES: find a family of curves X_p (genus ≥ 2, or of general type) whose extra rational/integral points are forced by ES failure at p; uniform finiteness would bound the failures.
why: Moves ES to finiteness of the exceptional set — a big intermediate step (finite exceptions + verification would finish).
first_step: Look for curves in the ES surface family U_p (e.g. intersections with x = λy) whose integral points correspond to certificates; compute genera.

title: 'At most one exception' phase: repulsion between ES-failing primes
connection: Heilbronn–Linfoot/Tatuzawa proved there is at most one exceptional discriminant before the full class-number-one solution. ES intermediate: show two (★)-failing or ES-failing primes p, p′ in a range [X, X²] cannot coexist (repulsion), e.g. because their characters would both be exceptional.
why: Finiteness/at-most-one statements are the classical stepping stone between almost-all and every.
first_step: Check the 14 (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰ for pairwise relations (p′/p) = 1, shared quadratic-residue profiles, and spacing; compare with random primes having the same individual profiles.

title: Geometric cancellation via trace functions for divisor-class sums
connection: Deligne's Ramanujan bound comes from geometry (purity). The ES deviation involves sums over characters of order ≥ 3 mod 4C of σ_χ(4Cp+1); for prime moduli these are sums of trace functions (Kummer sheaves) where Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel give square-root cancellation in long sums.
why: If the ES non-genus part X(p) can be written as a sum of trace functions with conductor bounded independently of p, Deligne-type bounds apply pointwise.
first_step: Restrict to prime levels 4C → prime e (windows) and write the e-slice certificate count as a trace-function sum over divisors; compute the conductors.

title: Lower bound by upper bounds on complements (Stepanov/Weil principle)
connection: In the elementary proofs of Weil's bound, the lower bound for N comes from upper bounds applied to complementary objects. ES: find a family {R_j(p)} with R_0 = R(p) whose total Σ_j R_j(p) has a pointwise asymptotic and whose other members have sharp pointwise upper bounds; then R(p) ≥ total − Σ_{j≠0} upper bounds.
why: Upper bounds for divisor counts in fixed classes (Shiu/Brun–Titchmarsh type) are much easier than lower bounds; the total over all classes (τ(4Cp+1) summed over C) has a known asymptotic.
first_step: Quantify at small levels (C ≤ 8, where φ(4C) ≤ 16): total τ-sum asymptotic vs. best upper bounds for each wrong class; how sharp must the upper bounds be for R(p) > 0 to follow?

title: Weyl/van der Corput differencing on the exponential-sum form of R(p)
connection: Weyl upgraded to every irrational polynomial by differencing. R(p) = Σ_{u,B} (4uB)⁻¹ Σ_{h mod 4uB} e(h(p+u+B)/(4uB)); apply van der Corput differencing in u (or B) to the nonzero frequencies to extract cancellation for fixed p in smoothed ranges.
why: Standard tool not obviously tried at fixed p; at least gives the true size of the error term in smoothed (★) counts.
first_step: Run the differencing on a smoothed model and compare the predicted error with the numerically observed |R_w(p) − M_w(p)|.

title: Large-p regime split by arithmetic configuration
connection: Tao handled different limiting zero configurations by different arguments. Split large p by configuration: (i) ℓ(p) small, (ii) ℓ(p) large but some small window works, (iii) (·/p) mimics a fixed character on all primes ≤ (log p)^A, … and design one certificate family per regime.
why: Each regime has extra structure to exploit; only finitely many regimes are needed if the split is by bounded data plus one 'pretentious' case.
first_step: Define the regime map on primes ≤ 10⁹ and check which certificate family is most robust in each regime.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Fourier reduction of an ES obstruction to a multiplicative (character) obstruction
connection: Tao reduced EDP to completely multiplicative functions by Fourier analysis. ES failure at window e means no divisor ratio ≡ −1 (mod e); reduce this to the existence of a character (or approximate homomorphism) χ mod e with χ(−1) = −1 that is 'large' on the prime factors of N_e.
why: If every obstruction is character-like, the problem becomes one about Legendre/higher-order characters at p — the BM/genus language where tools exist.
first_step: Prove the reduction for prime e: if the ±1-subset products of {g_i} miss −1, is there a character χ with χ(−1) = −1 and Σ_i Re χ(g_i) large? Test on data.

title: Dimension-zero exceptional set as an intermediate target
connection: Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss showed Littlewood's exceptional set has Hausdorff dimension 0 via measure rigidity. ES analogue: E(N) ≪ N^ε (zero 'dimension') — strictly between the current N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) and finiteness.
why: A measure-rigidity or entropy approach might reach 'dimension 0' even if CRT sieves stop at exponent 3/4 (EXCEPTIONAL_KARY3).
first_step: Formulate the profinite/adelic dynamical system whose invariant measures would control ES exceptions and check whether an entropy argument bounds the counting dimension of the exceptional set.

title: Real-variable circle method for 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p
connection: Count near-solutions via ∫ S(α)³ e(−4α/p) K(α) dα with S(α) = Σ_{x≤X} e(α/x) (van der Corput sums of smooth phases); exact solutions need tolerance ~ 1/(pxyz), far below what such integrals resolve.
why: Not nonsense: it gives the density of near-solutions and the scale at which arithmetic must take over; it locates the 'resolution gap' quantitatively.
first_step: Estimate the number of triples with |1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 4/p| < δ as a function of δ via the integral and compare with exact counts for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Goldfeld–Gross–Zagier-type effectivity: an auxiliary L-function with a high-order zero
connection: Goldfeld showed that an L-function with a zero of order ≥ 3 at s = 1/2 makes Siegel effective (Gross–Zagier supplied it). For an ineffective ES theorem (via Siegel), an analogous auxiliary object with a forced high-order vanishing would make p₀ explicit.
why: Only relevant once an ineffective all-large-p ES theorem exists, but it shows the route from ineffective to effective is not blocked in principle.
first_step: List places where Siegel's theorem could enter an ES argument (main-term lower bounds via L(1,χ)) and check whether Goldfeld's effective bound (h(−d) ≫ log d) is enough there.

title: Special-function positivity (Askey–Gasper) for weighted ES counts
connection: de Branges reduced every n to the Askey–Gasper positivity of Jacobi-polynomial sums. Seek weights w_C on levels such that Σ_C w_C · D_C(p) is expressible as a positive combination of 'basis' quantities via a classical positivity identity (e.g. Fejér kernels, Jacobi sums), valid for all p.
why: Every-n positivity theorems often reduce to one special-function inequality; ES weighted counts have explicit Fourier expansions over characters.
first_step: Write the character expansion of Σ_C w_C D_C(p) and search for weights making the coefficient vector positive-definite (Bochner/Fejér-type), at least in a model where p's character values are free.

title: Logarithmic density as an intermediate notion for ES-type sub-routes
connection: Tao's Collatz and Chowla results hold in logarithmic density, which is easier than natural density. For ES sub-routes whose failure sets might be infinite (e.g. (★) alone), compute logarithmic-density statements and the corresponding 'log-averaged' tools (Tao's entropy decrement).
why: Log-averaging made several almost-all results possible where natural density was stuck; useful for sub-route exceptional sets.
first_step: Estimate Σ_{p ≤ X, (★) fails} 1/p numerically and check whether log-averaged tools give a finite bound.
refs: arXiv:1909.03562 (Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values)

title: Parity of Ω(4Cp+1) and certificate existence
connection: Chen's theorem lives at the parity barrier (P₂ but not primes). Certificates at level C need a divisor in a class; if 4Cp+1 is prime, the only divisors are 1 and itself (class 1), so prime values of 4Cp+1 are useless. Measure the dependence of certificate probability on Ω(4Cp+1).
why: Tells whether ES needs 'many prime factors' (sieve-friendly almost-primes in reverse) and quantifies the loss from prime values.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁹ and C ≤ 10⁵ tabulate P(certificate at C | Ω(4Cp+1) = k) for k = 1..8.

title: Extreme-value statistics of the least certificate parameter
connection: Linnik-type theorems bound the least prime in a class. Measure the least certificate parameter (least C for (★), least e for windows) as p grows and fit an extreme-value law; a provable bound of the observed shape would be the 'Linnik constant' of ES.
why: Calibrates which quantitative statements are plausible (e.g. C(p) ≤ (log p)^A for all p?) before trying to prove any.
first_step: From the repo's census (and adversarial primes at 10¹⁸–10²⁵) tabulate max over p ≤ X of least C and least e versus log X.

title: Vinogradov's smooth-number trick for divisor classes
connection: Vinogradov bounded n(p): if every ℓ ≤ y is a QR, all y-smooth numbers are QRs, contradicting character-sum bounds since smooth numbers are plentiful. ES: if level C fails, no divisor of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 (mod 4C); if additionally we know the classes of small primes, smooth parts of 4Cp+1 are constrained. Count C for which 4Cp+1 has a y-smooth divisor in a forced class.
why: Transfers a proven every-p argument shape (n(p) bounds) to divisor classes, using smooth numbers in APs (Granville, Harper).
first_step: Model: fix the classes mod 4C of primes ≤ y; count C ≤ X such that 4Cp+1 has a y-smooth divisor d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) using smooth-number distribution; compare with data.

title: Prime-capture problems: every prime is caught by an infinite family of Chebotarev conditions
connection: A finite family of congruence conditions catches every large prime only if it contains all coprime classes modulo some M (Dirichlet), and finite families of splitting conditions can catch all primes only in special configurations (e.g. ℚ(√2), ℚ(√3), ℚ(√6) — reviewer example); bounded-modulus ES congruence families provably miss the square classes; ES Type II (abelian conditions p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB) and Type I (dihedral conditions via ring class fields) are infinite families with conductors up to ≍ p. List known 'every prime is captured by a family with conductor ≤ f(p)' theorems (e.g. least non-residue: some ℓ ≤ p^{0.152} has (p/ℓ) = −1) and place ES among them.
why: Identifies the closest proven 'prime-capture' statements and how their conductor bounds compare with what ES needs.
first_step: Write the conductor/size of the capturing family for ES sub-routes and for known capture theorems (Burgess, Linnik, Vinogradov) in one table.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x^2 + ny^2 (1989)

title: Large prime factors in the AP {4Cp + 1 : C ≤ K} (Sylvester–Schur/Shorey–Tijdeman)
connection: Sylvester–Schur: products of consecutive integers have a large prime factor; Shorey–Tijdeman extend to AP terms. For ES, a single prime q | 4Cp+1 with q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is a certificate. Large prime factors are guaranteed in the product over C ≤ K; the class condition q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is the extra requirement.
why: Gives a guaranteed supply of large prime divisors; the problem reduces to a class-distribution question for these forced large primes.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁹, list the largest prime factor of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10⁴ and test the rate at which it is ≡ −1 (mod 4C) against 2/φ(4C)-type models.
refs: Erdos, J. London Math. Soc. 9 (1934) 282-288 (A theorem of Sylvester and Schur)

title: Exceptional set of the two-term step is tiny: 'almost all two-term + rescue' structure
connection: Goldbach–Linnik used that the binary Goldbach exceptional set is small enough for a sparse rescue set. In ES, the two-term step m/N = 1/y + 1/z (after choosing x) fails on a thin set of (m, N); show that for every p, among the ≍ p choices of x the pairs (m_x, N_x) cannot all lie in that thin set, using its explicit structure.
why: The thin exceptional set of the two-term problem is explicit (divisor-class avoidance), so 'cannot all avoid' is a concrete combinatorial statement.
first_step: Characterise {(m, N) : m/N not a sum of two unit fractions} for small m and compute the fraction of x ∈ (p/4, p/2) for which (4x − p, px) lands in it, for hard p.

title: Multiplicative-function structure of the level indicator at fixed p
connection: MR's method uses multiplicativity in n. At fixed p, the function C ↦ D_C(p) is not multiplicative in C, but N ↦ 1[N has a divisor ≡ −1 mod t] is 'multiplicative-ish' in N for fixed t. Study the Dirichlet-series/Halász structure of n ↦ D_t^−(tn + 1) for fixed t (its mean value over n is controlled by Halász-type theorems).
why: Halász/MR techniques give 'every interval of length h' results for multiplicative functions; level-t certificate indicators along n might be accessible.
first_step: Express 1[D_t^−(tn+1) > 0] via the multiplicative set S_t and compute its mean in short intervals of n numerically; compare with Landau–Ramanujan-type predictions.
refs: arXiv:1501.04585 (Matomaki-Radziwill, Multiplicative functions in short intervals)

title: Auxiliary-prime choice with prescribed local behaviour for windows
connection: Shafarevich's embedding-problem induction succeeds by choosing auxiliary primes with prescribed local behaviour at each step. For ES windows, choose the window prime q with prescribed splitting behaviour in fields built from p (e.g. q splits in ℚ(√p, i) or has given Frobenius in a Kummer extension) so that Rat_q(K) is forced to contain −1.
why: Chebotarev guarantees auxiliary primes with any prescribed Frobenius; if the window certificate were a Frobenius condition, existence would follow.
first_step: Test whether success of window q for p is predicted by the Frobenius of q in ℚ(ζ_8, √p) or in Kummer fields ℚ(ζ_4, p^{1/4}).
refs: Neukirch-Schmidt-Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Ch. IX

title: Uniformity obstruction for linear-forms-in-primes certificate schemes at fixed p
connection: For fixed p, ES has finitely many solutions with denominators bounded polynomially in p (not O(p²): z can be ≍ p⁴, reviewer example x = (p+3)/4, y = (px+2)/3, z = pxy/2 for p ≡ 5 mod 24), and a fixed certificate parametrisation with auxiliary primes typically needs prime tuples of linear forms in a box polynomial in p with coefficients depending on p (many-to-one parametrisations need separate care). Green–Tao–Ziegler asymptotics are not uniform in coefficients comparable to the box, so they do not apply directly (correcting the BHS item).
why: Records precisely why the conditional→unconditional (Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg) move does not transfer to ES as stated, and what uniformity would be needed.
first_step: State the needed uniform version: count of t ≤ T with L_i(t) all prime for forms with coefficients ≤ T^{1+ε}; compare with known uniform results (e.g. for a single form: Brun–Titchmarsh / Siegel–Walfisz ranges).
refs: arXiv:math/0404188 (Green-Tao, primes contain arbitrarily long APs)

title: Distribution of R(p) modulo small primes ℓ (Ono-style equidistribution vs bias)
connection: Ono/Ahlgren studied p(n) modulo m: every residue class occurs. For ES, study R(p)/2 mod ℓ: equidistribution would be 'no structure', while a bias toward nonzero residues on some class would be a usable congruence. In particular check whether R(p)/2 ≡ 0 (mod ℓ) occurs with frequency ≈ 1/ℓ.
why: Cheap probe for hidden modular structure in the counts.
first_step: Compute the distribution of R(p)/2 mod 2, 3, 5, 7 over primes in each Mordell-hard class up to 10⁷.
refs: Ono, Ann. Math. 151 (2000) 293-307 (Distribution of the partition function modulo m)

title: Divisor sum over shifted primes reversed: Σ_{q prime} 1[q | p + m] for structured m
connection: The Titchmarsh divisor problem counts divisors of shifted primes. The trial form needs prime (or general) divisors of p + u in the class −1 mod (stuff tied to u); reverse the roles: for fixed p, count primes q ≡ 3 (4) with q | p + u and q = 4uC − 1 for some C — a 'Titchmarsh problem with a tied modulus' at a single p.
why: Relates single-prime certificates to the distribution of prime divisors of p + u, a classical object.
first_step: Count, for fixed p, pairs (u, q) with q | p + u, q ≡ −1 (mod 4u), q prime; compare with heuristic Σ_u τ*/φ(4u).

title: No minor arcs: positivity lets ES discard all but the smallest levels
connection: Goldbach-type proofs must bound minor arcs because terms cancel. ES counts are sums of nonnegative level counts, R(p) = Σ_C D_C(p) ≥ Σ_{C ≤ K} D_C(p); so ES ⟸ a certificate among levels C ≤ K = (log p)^A, where the expected count is still ≍ (log p)·(log K) → ∞. The whole problem is a lower bound for a short, explicit 'major-level' sum.
why: Reframes which part of the analytic machinery is needed: only lower bounds on a few explicit structured counts, no cancellation estimates for the bulk.
first_step: For p in the hard lists, find the least K(p) such that some level ≤ K(p) carries a certificate, and fit K(p) against (log p)^A.

title: Baseline: a single level already gives density one
connection: Level C = 1 works for p iff 4p + 1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) (it then automatically has two, so both cofactors are ≥ 3); the primes p for which 4p + 1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) have density zero (an upper-bound sieve gives ≪ X/(log X)^{3/2}; the matching order is the heuristic — check a source for the asymptotic). So 'almost all p' is cheap; all information sits in how fast the exceptional set of K levels decays.
why: A sanity baseline for every almost-all statement in this list: improvements must be measured in exceptional-set decay, not in 'density one'.
first_step: Compute the counting function of primes failing all levels C ≤ K for K = 1..10 up to 10⁹ and fit X/(log X)^{α_K}; compare α_K with Σ_{C≤K} δ_C from Landau–Ramanujan-type densities.

title: Affine-sieve strengthening: certificates with prime or almost-prime parameters
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak's affine sieve produces almost-primes in orbits once expansion is known. Ask whether every p has a (★) certificate with u, B (or 4uC − 1, 4BC − 1) prime or with ≤ r prime factors; if true numerically, sieve methods on the word set apply and the strengthened statement has more structure.
why: Strengthenings with prime parameters connect ES to the affine-sieve toolkit and to Chen-type almost-prime results.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁸ compute the least r such that a certificate with Ω(4uC − 1) ≤ r and Ω(4BC − 1) ≤ r exists; find primes needing large r.

title: Which almost-all ES results are sharp in the Kolmogorov sense?
connection: Kolmogorov's divergent Fourier series shows some a.e. theorems are optimal. For each ES-type almost-all theorem (single levels, (★), b=1, ES₅), decide whether infinitely many failures are known/expected (then the almost-all result is 'sharp') or not; only the latter are candidates for every-p upgrades.
why: Avoids attempting upgrades of statements that are actually false infinitely often (like single-level or (★)-only versions may be).
first_step: For each sub-route, estimate Σ_p P(fail) under the calibrated model; classify as 'expected finitely many' vs 'expected infinitely many' failures.
refs: Kolmogorov, Fund. Math. 4 (1923)/ C. R. 1926 (everywhere divergent L^1 Fourier series)

title: Zero-free region analogue: a range of levels where no 'conspiracy' is possible
connection: Linnik's theorem uses a zero-free region near s = 1 for all characters of modulus ≤ Q. For ES, find a range of small levels (C ≤ C₀(p)) where the relevant characters (mod 4C) are so few that a full conspiracy against certificates would force p into explicit square-like residue classes (contradiction for non-squares).
why: Small levels have few characters; a 'no conspiracy at small levels' lemma would be the ES zero-free region.
first_step: For C ≤ 30, characterise the residues of p (mod lcm(4C)) for which all these levels fail; compute the density of such residues and whether they are squares.

title: ES over a Dedekind domain with infinitely many units but no order: positivity replaced by a norm bound
connection: Replace the cone by 'all |x|_v ≥ 1 at archimedean places' (a norm-bounded set, not multiplicatively closed by inverses). This is the 'height-positivity' world: denominators must have all conjugates ≥ 1.
why: Unlike totally positive, this excludes small units; it may restore lottery behaviour in fields with units, giving hard twins with richer arithmetic.
first_step: In Z[√2], require |x|, |x'| ≥ 1 and search ES for rational p ≤ 10^4; compare with the totally-positive collapse.

title: Weil restriction view: ES over O_K for rational n = system of ES-like equations over Z in [K:Q] variables
connection: Writing x_i = a_i + b_i√D turns the O_K equation into two integer equations (rational and irrational parts) in six variables. Prop 3.3 solutions give an explicit family of integer points on this 6-variable variety.
why: The 6-variable integer variety contains the ES surface (b_i = 0); proved points on it might deform (via an integral curve) toward b_i = 0.
first_step: Write the two equations, then look for curves through the Prop 3.3 points meeting the b = 0 locus.

title: Arithmetic-progression denominators x, y, z in AP never occur (p < 4000)
connection: No solution with y − x = z − y appears for any p. Possibly a provable impossibility (or extreme rarity) via the equation 4x(x+d)(x+2d) = p(…)
why: AP-structured denominators connect to elliptic curves (the equation becomes a curve in (x,d) for fixed p); impossibility would be an elliptic-curve rank/torsion statement.
first_step: Write 4/p = 1/x + 1/(x+d) + 1/(x+2d) as a cubic curve in (x, d) and test for rational points; check whether a local obstruction rules it out.
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)

title: Brieskorn–Pham log canonical thresholds: ES ⇔ 4/n = lct(x^a + y^b + z^c)
connection: For the diagonal singularity x^a + y^b + z^c, lct = min(1, 1/a + 1/b + 1/c). So ES(n) ⇔ 4/n (< 1 for n ≥ 5) is the log canonical threshold of a 3-variable Brieskorn–Pham polynomial.
why: Birational geometry studies the set LCT₃ of 3-dimensional lcts (ACC, accumulation points); ES asks whether all 4/n lie in the Brieskorn–Pham stratum. Other quasi-homogeneous types give natural relaxations.
first_step: Check the known description of LCT for quasi-homogeneous isolated singularities in 3 variables (Arnold's types) and list which rationals arise from each type.

title: Platonic-style Euler equation 1/p + 1/q = 1/2 + 1/E as the 2-term cousin
connection: Regular maps {p,q} satisfy 1/p + 1/q − 1/2 = χ/(2E). Two-term Egyptian equations arise from Euler's formula; ES is the analogous three-type (hypermap) equation.
why: Suggests that ES-type equations with an extra 'defect' term are realizable by maps on surfaces with prescribed χ; maps exist abundantly, so realizability is not the issue — the integrality is.
first_step: Context only; record the hypermap equation N/x + N/y + N/z − N = χ as the general form.
